V=\text{Span}{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]}

examples.problem:
Consider the subspace $V$ and an orthogonal basis $\mathcal B$ of $V,$ given below. Given that $\mathcal B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\dfrac{a}{c}?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070290/assets/8f4bdd28c709b7f1b162e98ad196547f90c577df74e52fb6eef1d88efa209af9.png)
examples.worked_solution:
First, let's denote

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070290/assets/948d731d51fff2a1462db9eacab511eefbfdb1634bc9c45b2cf92ca67c4a4d18.png)

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

- **Step 1**: We set ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070290/assets/e8a3c7b01b547745c01f123634ca06ffc966ef9acec682af33f05066e00ceef1.png)

- **Step 2**: Next, we find $\mathbf{v}_2$, using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for $\mathbf v_2$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{(-3)\cdot 1+5\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{7}{3} \\ \frac{13}{3} \\ \frac{10}{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070290/assets/bb718fb5d9931c6f99268f40bbef401b50dc160304b271bd2035528bddabdec0.png) is an orthogonal basis for $V.$

Finally, $a=-\dfrac 7 3,$ $c=\dfrac{10}{3}$ and  

$$
\dfrac{a}{c} = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{7}{3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)} = -\dfrac{7}{10}.
$$
